blocks.text: **Cushing's syndrome** is the clinical state produced by **prolonged, inappropriately high glucocorticoid (cortisol) activity**, whatever the source. By far the **commonest cause overall is iatrogenic** — long-term synthetic steroids such as prednisolone. **Endogenous (spontaneous) Cushing's is rare**, with fewer than 5 new cases per million people per year.

**Syndrome vs disease:** _Cushing's syndrome_ is the clinical picture from any cause. _Cushing's disease_ is one specific cause — an **ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma**. Every patient with Cushing's disease has the syndrome, but not the other way round.

blocks.title: Classification of endogenous Cushing's syndrome (Davidson)
rows: Small-cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid, other neuroendocrine tumours; commoner in men
Usually large (> 5 cm) with other features of malignancy
Also aberrant adrenal receptors (e.g. GIP, catecholamines) and germline protein kinase A changes

blocks.title: Sources of ectopic ACTH
items: **Small-cell lung carcinoma** — the commonest paraneoplastic cause
**Bronchial carcinoid** and other neuroendocrine tumours (e.g. of pancreas or thymus)
Occult tumours such as **medullary thyroid carcinoma**
The tumour lies outside the pituitary, so its ACTH output **escapes cortisol negative feedback**

blocks.title: Pseudo-Cushing's states (cortisol excess without a tumour)
items: **Alcohol excess** — can mimic Cushing’s both clinically and biochemically; everything settles once drinking stops
**Major depressive illness** — biochemical abnormalities only, with some clinical overlap
**Primary obesity** — mild biochemical changes, some clinical overlap

blocks.text: **Always take a full drug history first.** Even **inhaled or topical** steroids can cause Cushing's in susceptible people. An inhaled steroid combined with a strong **CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ritonavir** can produce severe iatrogenic Cushing's.

**The percentages differ between books.** Davidson's text says pituitary disease is ~80% of endogenous cases, while its classification box gives 80% for _all_ ACTH-dependent causes (pituitary ~70%, ectopic ~10%). KC Essentials says about two-thirds are pituitary; Step-Up quotes ectopic ACTH at 10–15% and adrenal tumours at ~20%. For the exam: **pituitary is the commonest endogenous cause, adrenal ~20%, ectopic ~10%.**

**Cushing's disease** means cortisol excess driven by **inappropriate ACTH secretion from the pituitary** — usually a corticotroph **adenoma**, less often corticotroph hyperplasia. The constant ACTH drive causes **bilateral adrenal hyperplasia**, and adrenal androgen excess is common. It is the **second commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome** after steroid therapy, and the **commonest endogenous cause**. It is about **four times more frequent in women**.

blocks.title: Key features of the tumour
items: Usually a **microadenoma (< 10 mm)**, so **mass effects are rare** — hypopituitarism, visual field loss and stalk-disconnection hyperprolactinaemia are unusual
On classical staining it is a **basophil** adenoma (prolactin/GH tumours are acidophil; chromophobe tumours are usually non-functioning)
Pituitary MRI finds only **about 60%** of ACTH-secreting microadenomas
The tumour keeps **partial sensitivity to cortisol negative feedback**, so **high-dose dexamethasone suppresses** ACTH and cortisol and **CRH stimulates** ACTH — unlike ectopic tumours

blocks.text: A **random cortisol is of no diagnostic value** when Cushing's is suspected — cortisol varies through the day (highest on waking, lowest at night) and rises with any stress. Diagnosis rests on **dynamic tests**, mainly dexamethasone suppression.

Because pituitary tumours keep partial feedback, ACTH and cortisol in Cushing's disease are usually **lower than in ectopic ACTH syndrome**, which is why classic slow-onset Cushingoid features (rather than cachexia) are typical.

blocks.note: Look at: the hypothalamic CRH → pituitary ACTH (and MSH) → adrenal cortisol axis that a corticotroph adenoma over-drives.

blocks.text: Normally **over 95% of circulating cortisol is protein-bound**, mainly to corticosteroid-binding globulin (**CBG**, which oestrogens increase); only the **free fraction is active**. Cortisol can bind the **mineralocorticoid receptor**, but in MR-containing cells such as the kidney it is normally inactivated to cortisone by **11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)**.

blocks.title: From excess cortisol (or ACTH) to clinical feature
rows: Thin skin, easy bruising, purple striae, proximal myopathy, osteoporosis
Very high cortisol saturates renal 11β-HSD2 → cortisol activates the MR
Hypokalaemic alkalosis, which worsens myopathy and hyperglycaemia (less insulin secretion)
High ACTH acting on melanocortin 1 receptors in skin
Hirsutism, acne; androgen excess mainly in ACTH-dependent forms. Severe hirsutism or virilisation also suggests an adrenal tumour (Kumar)

blocks.title: Feedback and ACTH by cause
rows: No pigmentation; the opposite adrenal is suppressed (may stay so for a year or more after surgery)
Low endogenous cortisol and adrenal androgens

blocks.text: **Pigmentation reflects ACTH, not cortisol.** It appears only in ACTH-dependent disease, most strikingly in ectopic ACTH syndrome — never with an adrenal tumour or steroid therapy.

In **iatrogenic Cushing's there is no androgen excess**: the exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH, so adrenal androgen production falls. Virilisation in a woman points to an ACTH-dependent cause or, per Kumar, an adrenal tumour.

**Why is potassium low?** Davidson explains hypokalaemia by very high cortisol **overwhelming renal 11β-HSD2** (typical of ectopic ACTH). Zero to Finals mentions an adrenal adenoma that also secretes aldosterone — possible, but not the main mechanism. Follow Davidson.

blocks.note: Look at: masculinisation from androgen excess in a 46,XX patient — seen only in ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.

blocks.title: Features of glucocorticoid excess
rows: Central (truncal) obesity, buffalo hump, round plethoric moon face, thin limbs from muscle wasting
Thin skin, easy bruising, wide purple striae (abdomen, breasts, thighs), acne, hirsutism, poor wound healing
Proximal (thigh) myopathy; osteoporosis with vertebral and rib fractures, loss of height, back pain; avascular necrosis of the femoral head (especially exogenous steroids)
Oligo- or amenorrhoea, low libido, infertility
Cataracts, peptic ulcer, infections with little inflammatory response; growth arrest in children

blocks.text: Obesity, hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis are **non-specific**. In an obese patient the features that best favour true Cushing's are **easy bruising, proximal myopathy and thin skin** (plus typical purple striae). Any one feature alone has a low positive predictive value.

blocks.title: Clinical clues to the cause
rows: Short history, weight loss/cachexia, pigmentation, marked hypokalaemia, diabetes, very high ACTH; commoner in men
Malignant ectopic ACTH (e.g. small-cell lung cancer)
Classic, slowly developing Cushingoid features in ectopic ACTH syndrome (benign ectopic tumours can mimic pituitary disease clinically and biochemically)
Less aggressive ectopic source, e.g. bronchial carcinoid
Slow onset of typical features in a woman (4 : 1 female predominance)

blocks.text: Mnemonic **CUSHINGOID**: Cataracts, Ulcers, Skin changes (striae, bruising, thinning), Hypertension/Hirsutism, Infections, Necrosis of the femoral head, Glycosuria, Osteoporosis/Obesity, Immunosuppression, Diabetes. Old photographs help date the onset.

Glucocorticoid therapy itself **raises the white count (mainly neutrophils)** — do not mistake it for infection. Steroid-treated patients also **fracture at a higher bone density** than people with postmenopausal osteoporosis.

blocks.note: Look at: the summary of Cushing's features, and the same patient before and 1 year after trans-sphenoidal removal of a microadenoma.
Look at: the full list of symptoms and signs; the bold italic ones are those that best separate Cushing's from simple obesity and hirsutism.
Look at: the signs printed in bold — the most useful ones for telling Cushing's from simple obesity.
Look at: the physical findings of Cushing syndrome on one figure — useful for spotters.

blocks.text: Diagnosis is **two-step**: first **prove cortisol excess** (Cushing's syndrome), then **find the cause**. Exclude exogenous steroids first, and **avoid testing during acute illness or stress**, which activates the HPA axis and gives false results. No single test is perfect, so tests are combined.

blocks.title: Step 1 — confirming Cushing's syndrome (need two concordant abnormal tests)
rows: 1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00; serum cortisol at 09:00
Simple screening test; more false positives
Very sensitive (> 97%); KC calls it the most reliable screen
Loss of circadian rhythm in Cushing's
About 10% of patients are normal on some collections

blocks.title: Rules that catch people out
items: **Stop oestrogens (e.g. the pill) for 6 weeks** before testing: they raise CBG, and total-cortisol assays then give false positives
**Dexamethasone** is used because it does **not cross-react** in cortisol immunoassays; prednisolone may
A **09:00 cortisol < 100 nmol/L in a Cushingoid patient** suggests **exogenous synthetic steroid** (common) or cyclical endogenous Cushing’s (uncommon)
Cyclical secretion, obesity, depression and alcohol can all confuse the dynamic tests
Baseline tests in every case: **electrolytes, glucose, HbA1c and bone density**; FBC may show a raised white count

blocks.title: Step 2 — finding the cause
rows: ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic); values in between are a grey area
High-dose dexamethasone test (48 h of 2 mg every 6 h)
Favours Cushing's disease (about 90% of pituitary cases suppress)
> 20% rise in cortisol or > 50% rise in ACTH
Favours Cushing's disease; ectopic tumours rarely respond
Central : peripheral ACTH > 2 : 1 at baseline or > 3 : 1 after CRH
Best confirmation of Cushing's disease; may be skipped if MRI shows an adenoma > 6 mm
CXR, CT thorax and abdomen ± somatostatin (octreotide) scintigraphy
Search for an ectopic source; carcinoids can be tiny

blocks.alt: Algorithm: confirmed Cushing's syndrome → 09:00 ACTH. Suppressed ACTH → adrenal CT. High ACTH → pituitary pattern (HDDST suppression, CRH response, MRI adenoma, BIPSS gradient) means Cushing's disease; no suppression or CRH response → CT thorax/abdomen ± somatostatin scintigraphy for ectopic ACTH.

blocks.text: **Dexamethasone protocols differ between books.** Davidson screens with an overnight 1 mg test or a 48-h low-dose test (0.5 mg 6-hourly), and its high-dose test is **2 mg 6-hourly for 48 h**. Step-Up and Zero to Finals give single overnight doses: **1 mg** (low) and **8 mg** (high). The cut-offs agree: < 50 nmol/L (1.8 µg/dL) or < 2 µg/dL means normal suppression, and **> 50% suppression** on high dose favours pituitary disease. Use Davidson's protocol in written answers.
**Image only after the biochemistry has localised the problem.** Small incidental pituitary and adrenal lesions are common, and pituitary MRI misses about 40% of corticotroph microadenomas.

blocks.note: Look at: the sequence for confirming suspected Cushing’s — exclude steroids, then UFC, late-night salivary cortisol and ONDST/LDDST, needing two concordant abnormal results.
Look at: the branches from plasma ACTH to adrenal CT, pituitary tests (MRI, CRH, HDDST, BIPSS) or a search for an ectopic source.
Look at: the stepwise US-style diagnostic algorithm (overnight tests) to compare with Davidson’s.

blocks.text: Untreated severe Cushing's syndrome carries about a **50% 5-year mortality**, from venous thromboembolism, hypertension, myocardial infarction, infection and heart failure. **Control the cortisol excess medically before surgery or radiotherapy** in severe cases, titrating the drug against serum cortisol or 24-h urine free cortisol.

blocks.title: Treatment by cause
rows: ~70% immediate remission (Davidson; Kumar 75–80%); ~20% relapse, often years later → life-long follow-up
Pituitary radiotherapy, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenalectomy
Radiotherapy is slow and works in 50–60% of adults (80% of children)
Opposite adrenal may stay suppressed for a year or more → steroid cover
Poor prognosis; tumour-bed radiotherapy cuts local recurrence; mitotane plus chemotherapy, often with poor responses
Resect a localised tumour (e.g. bronchial carcinoid)
Incurable cancer: medical cortisol control or bilateral adrenalectomy
Reduce the steroid dose gradually where possible
Steroid-sparing agents (e.g. azathioprine); never stop long-term steroids abruptly

blocks.title: Drugs used in Cushing’s
rows: Usual first choice; 750 mg–4 g daily in 3–4 doses
200 mg three times daily; synergistic with metyrapone
Cushing's disease when surgery is unsuitable; twice-daily SC; hyperglycaemia common; cortisol rebounds when stopped

blocks.text: **Nelson's syndrome:** bilateral adrenalectomy cures ACTH-dependent Cushing's, but in pituitary disease the loss of cortisol feedback lets the corticotroph tumour grow — an **invasive macroadenoma** with **very high ACTH and marked pigmentation**. It follows about **20%** of adrenalectomies for Cushing's disease. Early pituitary radiotherapy may reduce the risk; treat with pituitary surgery and/or radiotherapy.

After successful selective adenomectomy the patient is almost always **ACTH-deficient** in the first days — a **good prognostic sign** that needs glucocorticoid cover. After bilateral adrenalectomy, steroid replacement is **life-long**.
**Remission figures differ:** Davidson gives ~70% immediate remission after trans-sphenoidal surgery (with ~20% later relapse); Kumar gives 75–80% overall. Quote Davidson's figure.

blocks.title: Glucocorticoid therapy — equivalent doses and bone protection
items: **Prednisolone 5 mg** ≈ hydrocortisone 20 mg ≈ **dexamethasone 0.5 mg** (and ≈ cortisone acetate 25 mg)
Consider **bone protection** if systemic steroids are expected for **more than 3 months**

blocks.text: An **adrenal incidentaloma** (found on ~4% of scans) needs a **dexamethasone suppression test** to exclude subclinical Cushing’s. Remove large (> 4–5 cm) or functioning tumours; observe small non-functioning ones.

cards.front: Commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome overall?
cards.back: Iatrogenic — long-term synthetic glucocorticoids such as prednisolone.

cards.front: Commonest endogenous cause of Cushing's syndrome?
cards.back: Cushing's disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) — about 70% of endogenous cases.

cards.front: Share of ACTH-independent endogenous Cushing’s, and its causes?
cards.back: About 20%: adrenal adenoma ~15%, adrenal carcinoma ~5%, rare nodular hyperplasias < 1%.
Alcohol excess (clinical + biochemical), major depression (biochemical), primary obesity (mild biochemical).

cards.front: Typical size of the tumour in Cushing's disease?
cards.back: Microadenoma < 10 mm — so mass effects are rare and MRI finds only ~60%.

cards.front: Mechanism of hypokalaemic alkalosis in severe Cushing's?
cards.back: Very high cortisol saturates renal 11β-HSD2, so cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor.

cards.front: Why are some Cushing's patients pigmented?
cards.back: High ACTH stimulates melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes — so pigmentation occurs only in ACTH-dependent causes.

cards.front: Signs that best favour Cushing’s over simple obesity?
cards.back: Easy bruising, proximal myopathy and thin skin (with purple striae).

cards.front: Clinical clues to malignant ectopic ACTH?
cards.back: Short history, weight loss/cachexia, pigmentation, hypokalaemia, diabetes, very high ACTH.
Two concordant abnormal tests of: low-dose dexamethasone suppression, late-night cortisol, 24-h urine free cortisol.

cards.front: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test: protocol and normal result?
cards.back: 1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00, cortisol at 09:00; normal < 50 nmol/L (1.8 µg/dL).

cards.front: Plasma ACTH cut-offs once Cushing's is confirmed?
cards.back: < 1.1 pmol/L → adrenal cause; > 3.3 pmol/L → pituitary or ectopic; in between = grey area.

cards.front: High-dose dexamethasone result that favours Cushing's disease?
cards.back: > 50% fall in cortisol from baseline (ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours do not suppress).

cards.front: Why stop the combined pill before cortisol testing?
cards.back: Oestrogen raises CBG, so total cortisol is falsely high — stop it for 6 weeks.

cards.front: Treatment of choice for Cushing's disease?
cards.back: Trans-sphenoidal selective adenomectomy — ~70% immediate remission, ~20% relapse, life-long follow-up.
Growth of a corticotroph tumour into an invasive macroadenoma with very high ACTH and pigmentation after bilateral adrenalectomy (~20%).
Blocks 11β-hydroxylase, reducing cortisol synthesis; used pre-operatively or when surgery fails.

cards.front: Prednisolone 5 mg is equivalent to how much hydrocortisone and dexamethasone?

questions.leadIn: Using the options, pair every patient with the cause that fits best. One option may suit several patients, or none.
options: Ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung carcinoma

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with HIV takes a ritonavir-boosted antiretroviral regimen and uses an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma. Over 3 months she develops a round red face, purple abdominal striae and easy bruising. Her 09:00 serum cortisol is 40 nmol/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: a Cushingoid patient with a **low morning cortisol** is taking an exogenous steroid, and **ritonavir (a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor)** stops the inhaled steroid being cleared, so enough reaches the circulation to cause severe iatrogenic Cushing’s.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks about 80 units of alcohol a week has a plethoric face and central obesity. His 24-hour urine free cortisol is raised and cortisol fails to suppress overnight with dexamethasone. After a month of supervised abstinence, his appearance improves and all tests become normal.
items.explanation: Alcohol excess can mimic Cushing’s **clinically and biochemically**; the clue is that everything **resolves on stopping alcohol**.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years has had 6 weeks of weight loss, weakness and darkening skin. Blood pressure is 172/98 mmHg and potassium 2.6 mmol/L. Plasma ACTH is markedly raised.
items.explanation: Rapid onset, weight loss, **pigmentation and hypokalaemia with very high ACTH** in an older male smoker is malignant ectopic ACTH — most often small-cell lung cancer. A carcinoid usually gives a slower, classic Cushingoid picture.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with Cushing's disease.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about her pituitary tumour is most likely to be true?
options: It is usually a macroadenoma causing bitemporal hemianopia
It is usually a microadenoma less than 10 mm across
It has completely lost feedback sensitivity to glucocorticoids
It usually causes hyperprolactinaemia by stalk compression
It can almost always be seen on pituitary MRI
questions.explanation: Corticotroph tumours in Cushing's disease are **usually microadenomas (< 10 mm)**, so mass effects such as field loss, hypopituitarism and disconnection hyperprolactinaemia are rare.
whyNot: Macroadenomas with field defects are rare in Cushing’s disease; the tumour is usually tiny.
Pituitary tumours keep **partial** feedback — the basis of high-dose dexamethasone suppression. Complete loss is typical of ectopic tumours.
Disconnection hyperprolactinaemia needs a large tumour; it is rare here.
MRI detects only about 60% of ACTH-secreting microadenomas.

questions.stem: A GP suspects Cushing's disease in a 36-year-old woman with central weight gain, bruising and proximal weakness. A random afternoon serum cortisol is within the reference range.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The result is uninformative; arrange dexamethasone suppression testing
The normal result confirms a pseudo-Cushing’s state
Start metyrapone and recheck in a month
questions.explanation: Cortisol varies through the day (highest on waking, lowest at night) and rises with stress, so a **random cortisol is of no value** in suspected Cushing's. Diagnosis rests on **dynamic tests** such as dexamethasone suppression.
whyNot: A random level can be normal in true Cushing’s; it excludes nothing.
Imaging comes only after biochemical confirmation and localisation.
Pseudo-Cushing’s also needs dynamic testing and a context (alcohol, depression); a random level shows nothing.
Treatment without a confirmed diagnosis is inappropriate.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with ectopic ACTH syndrome has a potassium of 2.4 mmol/L and a bicarbonate of 34 mmol/L. His plasma renin and aldosterone are both low.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism of his hypokalaemia?
options: Gastrointestinal potassium loss from tumour-related diarrhoea
Insulin-driven shift of potassium into cells
Poor dietary potassium intake from cachexia
questions.explanation: Very high cortisol levels **saturate renal 11β-HSD2**, so cortisol is no longer inactivated to cortisone and **acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor** — causing hypokalaemic alkalosis (and suppressed renin and aldosterone).
whyNot: Aldosterone is low, so this is not primary aldosteronism.
Diarrhoea would tend to cause acidosis, not alkalosis, and is not the described mechanism.
Cortisol excess reduces insulin secretion; an insulin shift is not the cause.
Low intake alone rarely causes such severe hypokalaemia with alkalosis.

questions.stem: Five patients have Cushing's syndrome from different causes.
questions.leadIn: Which patient is most likely to have skin hyperpigmentation?
options: A woman with a 3 cm cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
A man taking prednisolone 30 mg daily for a year
A man with ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung cancer
A woman with an adrenocortical carcinoma
A teenager with primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease
questions.explanation: Pigmentation is caused by **high ACTH acting on melanocortin 1 receptors**, so it occurs only in ACTH-dependent disease — most markedly **ectopic ACTH**, where ACTH levels are highest.
whyNot: Adrenal adenomas suppress ACTH, so there is no pigmentation.
Exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH.
Adrenal carcinoma is ACTH-independent; ACTH is suppressed.
Despite the name, the pigment is in the adrenal nodules; ACTH is suppressed and the skin is not pigmented.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, pair every patient with the cause that fits best. One option may suit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Clinical clues to the cause of Cushing’s syndrome
options: Ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung carcinoma

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has developed Cushingoid features over 6 months, along with severe hirsutism, a deepening voice and clitoral enlargement. Plasma ACTH is undetectable, and CT shows a 10 cm irregular right adrenal mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: undetectable ACTH means an **adrenal** cause, and severe hirsutism or virilisation also points to an adrenal tumour. The **large (> 5 cm), irregular mass** and rapid course mark it as **adrenocortical carcinoma** rather than an adenoma.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has a 3-year history of slowly worsening central obesity, purple striae, bruising and mild pigmentation. ACTH is high, cortisol does not suppress on high-dose dexamethasone, and there is no response to CRH. Pituitary MRI is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: high ACTH with **no suppression and no CRH response** means ectopic ACTH; the **slow, classic Cushingoid picture** suggests a less aggressive tumour such as a **bronchial carcinoid** rather than small-cell cancer.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a BMI of 41 kg/m² has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Her skin is not thin, she has no bruising, proximal power is normal, and an overnight dexamethasone test and 24-hour urine free cortisol are both normal.
items.explanation: Obesity, hypertension and diabetes are non-specific. Without the discriminating signs (bruising, thin skin, myopathy) and with **normal screening tests**, this is simple obesity.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, choose the most useful next test in every scenario. One option may suit several scenarios, or none.
questions.theme: Choosing the next test in suspected Cushing’s syndrome

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman's 24-hour urine free cortisol is raised on two collections and her cortisol fails to suppress on a low-dose dexamethasone test. She takes no steroids.
items.explanation: Two concordant abnormal tests **confirm Cushing’s syndrome**. The key next step is **plasma ACTH**, which splits ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has confirmed Cushing's syndrome. His morning plasma ACTH is below 1.1 pmol/L on two occasions.
items.explanation: Undetectable ACTH means **ACTH-independent (adrenal)** disease, so image the **adrenals with CT**.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. Pituitary MRI is normal and the high-dose dexamethasone and CRH tests give equivocal results.
items.explanation: MRI misses many microadenomas. **BIPSS** (central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient) is the best way to confirm a pituitary source when the other tests are inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman had a bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease 4 years ago and takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She now has progressive darkening of the skin, headaches and loss of the outer halves of both visual fields.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrent Cushing’s disease from adrenal rest tissue
questions.explanation: After bilateral adrenalectomy for pituitary disease, **loss of cortisol feedback** lets the corticotroph tumour enlarge into an **invasive macroadenoma** with **very high ACTH (pigmentation)** and mass effects — **Nelson's syndrome** (~20% of cases).
whyNot: Under-replacement can raise ACTH and pigmentation, but would not cause an expanding pituitary mass with field loss.
Recurrent cortisol excess would give Cushingoid features, not just pigmentation with a pituitary mass.
An ectopic tumour would not explain the pituitary mass effects after treatment of a known pituitary adenoma.
A non-functioning adenoma would not cause marked pigmentation.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with severe Cushing's disease is awaiting trans-sphenoidal surgery. His potassium is 2.8 mmol/L and glucose 16 mmol/L. The team want to lower his cortisol for a few weeks before the operation.
questions.leadIn: Which drug, an 11β-hydroxylase inhibitor, is most often used?
questions.explanation: **Metyrapone blocks 11β-hydroxylase** and is the usual drug to control cortisol before surgery, titrated against serum or urine cortisol.
whyNot: Mitotane is an adrenolytic used for adrenocortical carcinoma.
Dopamine agonists rarely control Cushing’s disease.
Spironolactone may help potassium but does not reduce cortisol.
Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid and would add to the excess.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, pair every set of results with its best explanation. One option may suit several cases, or none.
questions.theme: Interpreting cortisol and ACTH test patterns

items.stem: Cortisol fails to suppress on a 48-hour low-dose dexamethasone test. Morning ACTH is 12 pmol/L. On the high-dose test cortisol falls by 75% from baseline, and IV CRH produces a 40% rise in cortisol.
items.explanation: ACTH-dependent (ACTH > 3.3 pmol/L), with **> 50% high-dose suppression** and a **CRH response**: the tumour keeps partial feedback, so it is pituitary.

items.stem: Cortisol suppresses neither on low-dose nor on high-dose dexamethasone. Morning ACTH is 0.6 pmol/L on two occasions.
items.explanation: Undetectable ACTH = **ACTH-independent** autonomous adrenal cortisol, which no dose of dexamethasone can suppress.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman taking the combined pill has no Cushingoid features. Her overnight dexamethasone test cortisol is 85 nmol/L. Six weeks after stopping the pill the repeat value is 30 nmol/L.
items.explanation: Oestrogen raises **CBG**, and assays measure total cortisol, giving a false-positive. After **6 weeks off oestrogen** the test is normal.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with a Cushingoid appearance has a 09:00 cortisol of 45 nmol/L and an undetectable ACTH. He applies a potent steroid cream to widespread psoriasis every day.
items.explanation: A **low morning cortisol in a Cushingoid patient** suggests an exogenous synthetic steroid; topical steroids can be absorbed enough to suppress ACTH and cortisol.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² is referred with possible Cushing’s syndrome.
questions.leadIn: Which clinical finding would most strongly favour true Cushing’s syndrome over simple obesity?
questions.explanation: In an obese patient, **proximal myopathy, easy bruising and thin skin** are the features that best favour Cushing's. The others are common in simple obesity.
whyNot: Central obesity is common in simple obesity.
Hypertension is non-specific.
Glucose intolerance is common with obesity alone.
Hirsutism is common in obese women without Cushing’s.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill is to be tested for suspected Cushing's syndrome.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate step before dexamethasone suppression testing?
options: Proceed now, as the pill does not affect cortisol assays
Stop the pill for 6 weeks before testing
Measure a random afternoon cortisol instead
Double the dexamethasone dose to overcome the oestrogen
Use prednisolone instead of dexamethasone for the test
questions.explanation: Oestrogens raise **CBG**, and most assays measure total cortisol, so the test may be falsely positive. Stop oestrogens **for 6 weeks** first.
whyNot: Oestrogen does affect total cortisol through CBG.
Random cortisol is of no value in Cushing’s.
Increasing the dose does not correct the CBG effect and changes the test.
Prednisolone can cross-react in cortisol immunoassays; dexamethasone is used because it does not.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has confirmed Cushing's disease with a 7 mm adenoma on pituitary MRI.
questions.leadIn: What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: **Trans-sphenoidal selective removal of the adenoma** by an experienced surgeon is the treatment of choice — about 70% go into immediate remission.
whyNot: Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort and risks Nelson’s syndrome.
Radiotherapy is slow, effective in only 50–60%, and mainly used after failed surgery.
Metyrapone controls cortisol but does not treat the tumour; used before surgery or if surgery fails.
Dopamine agonists are rarely effective.

questions.stem: A patient taking prednisolone 5 mg daily needs to be switched to hydrocortisone at an equivalent glucocorticoid dose.
questions.leadIn: What daily dose of hydrocortisone is approximately equivalent?
questions.explanation: Approximate equivalents: **hydrocortisone 20 mg ≈ prednisolone 5 mg ≈ dexamethasone 0.5 mg** (cortisone acetate 25 mg).
whyNot: Hydrocortisone is about four times less potent than prednisolone.
Too low — this is half the equivalent dose.
This would be about twice the equivalent dose.
This would be about four times the equivalent dose.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old heavy smoker (30 per day) has had 2 months of weakness, 6 kg weight loss and darkening skin. BP is 170/100 mmHg. Potassium is 2.5 mmol/L, bicarbonate 35 mmol/L and glucose 15 mmol/L. Cortisol is very high and fails to suppress on high-dose dexamethasone; plasma ACTH is 60 pmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
options: Ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung carcinoma
Ectopic ACTH from a bronchial carcinoid
questions.explanation: **Step 1 — ACTH-dependent?** ACTH 60 pmol/L is far above 3.3 pmol/L, so yes; adrenal causes are out. **Step 2 — pituitary or ectopic?** No high-dose suppression means feedback is lost → ectopic. Very high ACTH explains the **pigmentation** and, with very high cortisol saturating 11β-HSD2, the **hypokalaemic alkalosis**. **Step 3 — which ectopic source?** The **short history and weight loss** in a heavy smoker point to a malignant tumour, small-cell lung cancer; carcinoids usually give a slower, classic Cushingoid picture.
whyNot: Pituitary tumours usually suppress on high-dose dexamethasone and rarely produce such high ACTH and rapid wasting.
Adrenal carcinoma suppresses ACTH, so it could not cause a high ACTH or pigmentation.
Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalaemic hypertension but not high cortisol, high ACTH or pigmentation.
Carcinoid-related ectopic ACTH is less aggressive and usually presents with slower, classic Cushingoid features.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has a moon face, purple striae and thin, bruised skin. Her 09:00 serum cortisol (normal sleep pattern) is 60 nmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** she looks Cushingoid, so something is activating glucocorticoid receptors. **Step 2:** yet her own morning cortisol is **low (< 100 nmol/L)**, so the excess glucocorticoid is not cortisol. **Step 3:** this pattern means an **exogenous synthetic steroid** (common) — or, uncommonly, cyclical endogenous Cushing’s caught in a quiet phase. **Next:** take a careful drug history including inhaled, topical and injected steroids.
whyNot: An adrenal adenoma produces cortisol, so morning cortisol would be high.
Cushing’s disease produces high cortisol.
Adrenal insufficiency gives a low cortisol but not a Cushingoid appearance.
Raised CBG would increase total cortisol, not lower it.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with bruising, proximal weakness and new hypertension takes no medication. Her overnight dexamethasone suppression test cortisol is 140 nmol/L, and her 24-hour urine free cortisol is above the reference range on two collections.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat the overnight test in 6 months
questions.explanation: **Step 1 — is it Cushing’s syndrome?** Two concordant abnormal tests (failure to suppress to < 50 nmol/L and raised urine free cortisol) confirm it. **Step 2 — what next?** The diagnosis is two-step: now find the cause, starting with **morning plasma ACTH**. Suppressed ACTH leads to adrenal imaging; high ACTH leads to pituitary versus ectopic tests. **Imaging comes only after** this biochemical localisation.
whyNot: Imaging the pituitary before showing ACTH dependence risks being misled by an incidental lesion.
Adrenal CT is used only once ACTH is shown to be suppressed.
The diagnosis is already confirmed; delay is not justified.
Random cortisol adds nothing.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, choose the best management for every patient. One option may suit several patients, or none.
options: Resection of the ACTH-secreting lung tumour
Gradual steroid reduction with a steroid-sparing agent

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome. CT shows a 3 cm smooth, homogeneous left adrenal mass and a normal right adrenal.
items.explanation: A benign-looking unilateral adrenal adenoma: **laparoscopic adrenalectomy** is the treatment of choice (with steroid cover, as the other adrenal is suppressed).

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has ectopic ACTH syndrome from metastatic small-cell lung cancer. His potassium is 2.3 mmol/L and he is profoundly weak. Chemotherapy is planned and he needs his cortisol controlled now.
items.explanation: The tumour is incurable, so the aim is to **control cortisol medically** — metyrapone blocks 11β-hydroxylase. Pasireotide is licensed for pituitary-dependent (Cushing's) disease.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has persistent Cushing's disease despite trans-sphenoidal surgery, later pituitary radiotherapy and a trial of steroidogenesis inhibitors that she could not tolerate. She wants definitive control of her cortisol excess.
items.explanation: When pituitary surgery, radiotherapy and medical therapy have failed, **bilateral adrenalectomy** is the effective last resort — with life-long replacement and surveillance for Nelson’s syndrome (her previous radiotherapy may lower that risk).

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has needed prednisolone 30 mg daily for 9 months to control severe Crohn’s disease and is now Cushingoid with striae and early osteopenia.
items.explanation: Iatrogenic Cushing’s: **reduce the steroid gradually** where possible and use a **steroid-sparing immunosuppressant** (e.g. azathioprine). Never stop long-term steroids abruptly — the suppressed axis cannot respond.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, choose the most useful investigation in every scenario. One option may suit several scenarios, or none.
questions.theme: Imaging and localisation in Cushing’s syndrome

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. Cortisol falls by 70% on high-dose dexamethasone and rises after CRH.
items.explanation: The biochemistry points to the **pituitary**, so image it with **MRI**; an adenoma > 6 mm may make BIPSS unnecessary.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has ACTH-dependent Cushing’s that does not suppress on high-dose dexamethasone and does not respond to CRH. CT of the chest and abdomen is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: the tests point to an **ectopic source**; when CT cannot find it, **somatostatin receptor scintigraphy** can show a small neuroendocrine tumour such as a carcinoid.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome. Electrolytes, glucose and HbA1c have been checked. Which further baseline test assesses an important complication?
items.explanation: Every patient needs **bone density measurement** at baseline, because cortisol excess causes osteoporosis and fractures.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman develops Cushingoid features after a year of high-dose prednisolone for lupus. Unlike her friend with Cushing’s disease, she has no acne or excess hair growth.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the absence of androgen excess?
options: Exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH, so adrenal androgen output falls
Prednisolone blocks androgen receptors in the skin
Prednisolone is converted to oestrogen in fat
Androgen excess appears only after 5 years of steroid use
questions.explanation: Adrenal androgens are driven by ACTH. **Exogenous steroids suppress ACTH**, so androgen production falls; androgen excess and virilisation are features of **ACTH-dependent** causes.
whyNot: Prednisolone is not an androgen-receptor antagonist.
There is no such conversion of prednisolone.
Lupus does not explain it, and adrenal failure would not give a Cushingoid picture.
Duration is not the explanation; the mechanism is ACTH suppression.

questions.stem: Three days after trans-sphenoidal removal of an ACTH-secreting microadenoma, a 37-year-old woman's 09:00 serum cortisol is undetectable. She feels tired and nauseated.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation?
options: Likely surgical cure; give glucocorticoid replacement
Surgery has failed; arrange bilateral adrenalectomy
Evidence of an additional ectopic ACTH source
questions.explanation: After successful selective adenomectomy the remaining normal corticotrophs are suppressed, so patients are almost always **ACTH-deficient** at first — a **good prognostic sign**. They need glucocorticoid cover until the axis recovers.
whyNot: Undetectable cortisol shows the tumour has been removed, not that surgery failed.
Nelson’s follows bilateral adrenalectomy, not pituitary surgery, and causes very high ACTH.
This is the expected finding; ignoring it risks adrenal crisis.
An ectopic source would keep cortisol high.

questions.stem: A patient with ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome has a CRH stimulation test.
questions.leadIn: Which result most strongly favours Cushing's disease over ectopic ACTH?
options: Cortisol rises by more than 20% from baseline
No change in ACTH or cortisol
questions.explanation: Pituitary corticotroph tumours still respond to CRH: a **> 20% rise in cortisol or > 50% rise in ACTH** favours Cushing’s disease. Ectopic tumours rarely respond.
whyNot: No response is the typical ectopic pattern.
A > 50% fall is the high-dose dexamethasone criterion, not a CRH response.
ACTH below 1.1 pmol/L indicates an adrenal cause, not a CRH response.
This is not how the CRH test is read.

questions.stem: A student asks why severe Cushing's syndrome should be treated promptly.
questions.leadIn: What is the approximate 5-year mortality of untreated severe Cushing’s syndrome?
questions.explanation: Untreated severe Cushing’s has about a **50% 5-year mortality**, mainly from thromboembolism, hypertension, MI, infection and heart failure.
whyNot: Far too low.
Too low.
Too low.
Too high.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, pair every patient with the complication that fits best. One option may suit several patients, or none.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has taken prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica for 2 years without bone protection. She has sudden severe mid-back pain after lifting a shopping bag and has lost 3 cm in height.
items.explanation: Long-term steroids cause **osteoporosis**, and steroid-treated patients fracture at higher bone density; sudden back pain with height loss is a vertebral collapse. Bone protection should be considered beyond 3 months.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man admitted with an asthma attack has had high-dose prednisolone for 3 days. He is afebrile and improving, with no focus of infection, but his white count is 15 × 10⁹/L, mainly neutrophils.
items.explanation: Glucocorticoids **raise the neutrophil count**; in a well, afebrile patient without a focus, this is a drug effect rather than infection.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman on long-term high-dose steroids for lupus has had 2 months of deep groin pain on walking.
items.explanation: Groin pain on walking in a patient on long-term **exogenous steroids** suggests **avascular necrosis of the femoral head**, a complication seen especially with exogenous steroid use.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with Cushing's disease who is unsuitable for surgery starts twice-daily subcutaneous pasireotide.
questions.leadIn: Which adverse effect is most commonly associated with this drug?
questions.explanation: Pasireotide, a **somatostatin analogue** that suppresses tumour ACTH, commonly causes **hyperglycaemia**. Cortisol tends to rebound when it is stopped.
whyNot: Not a recognised common effect of pasireotide.
Potassium is more likely to be low in Cushing’s; pasireotide is not linked to hyperkalaemia.
Not a recognised effect.
Not a recognised common effect.

questions.leadIn: Using the options, pair every patient with the diagnosis that fits best. One option may suit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 2 years of gradual weight gain, purple striae and irregular periods. Two screening tests are abnormal, morning ACTH is 8 pmol/L, cortisol falls by 65% on high-dose dexamethasone, and MRI shows an 8 mm pituitary lesion.
items.explanation: ACTH-dependent, suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone, with a pituitary lesion > 6 mm: **Cushing’s disease**.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has rapidly progressive Cushing's syndrome with undetectable ACTH. CT shows a 9 cm irregular left adrenal mass with features of malignancy.
items.explanation: Two steps: suppressed ACTH means an adrenal cause, and a **large (> 5 cm) mass with malignant features** means **adrenocortical carcinoma** rather than an adenoma.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome. CT shows both adrenal glands to be markedly enlarged and replaced by multiple large nodules.
items.explanation: Suppressed ACTH with **bilateral large nodular adrenals** fits ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (AIMAH) — a rare cause.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome with a normal pituitary MRI. She undergoes bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling.
questions.leadIn: Which result best confirms a pituitary source?
options: Central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio greater than 2 : 1 at baseline
Central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio of 1 : 1 at baseline
Peripheral ACTH higher than central ACTH
Equal central and peripheral ACTH after CRH
questions.explanation: A **central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient > 2 : 1 at baseline (or > 3 : 1 after CRH)** shows the pituitary is the source. BIPSS is the best confirmation of Cushing’s disease when MRI is unhelpful.
whyNot: No gradient suggests an ectopic source.
A higher peripheral level points away from the pituitary.
Below the > 3 : 1 post-CRH threshold — no pituitary gradient.
No gradient after CRH suggests ectopic ACTH.

ospe.identify: Cushingoid habitus: moon face, plethora, central obesity, striae and thin limbs — and resolution 1 year after trans-sphenoidal removal of a microadenoma (Cushing's disease).
Symptoms and signs of Cushing's syndrome (proximal myopathy, thin skin, bruising, purple striae, moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity) — know which best separate it from simple obesity.
Physical findings of Cushing syndrome shown on one figure — be ready to name each Cushingoid sign on a spotter.
Virilisation (masculinisation) of a 46,XX patient from adrenal androgen excess — Step-Up ties this to ACTH-dependent Cushing’s; it is not seen in iatrogenic Cushing’s, where ACTH is suppressed.
